title: The Gimli Glider
facts: 23 July 1983, Air Canada Flight 143, Boeing 767, Montreal to Edmonton. Fuel calculated in pounds instead of kilograms: about 10,100 kg on board instead of 22,300 kg needed. Both engines stopped at about 41,000 feet. Glass cockpit screens went dark; the ram air turbine dropped out to power hydraulics. Winnipeg was too far; first officer Maurice Quintal knew the former air force base at Gimli. The runway was being used for a car race with campers nearby. Captain Bob Pearson, an experienced glider pilot, used a forward slip to lose height. Nose gear collapsed, the jet scraped and stopped. All 69 people survived; about 10 minor injuries. The plane was repaired and flew until 2008.
sources: Wikipedia: Gimli Glider; Transportation Safety Board of Canada

title: Miracle on the Hudson
facts: 15 January 2009, US Airways Flight 1549, Airbus A320, from LaGuardia. Hit a flock of Canada geese at about 2,800 feet, both engines lost thrust. Less than four minutes from bird strike to landing. Captain Chesley 'Sully' Sullenberger and first officer Jeffrey Skiles decided they could not reach any airport and landed on the Hudson River near Midtown Manhattan. NY Waterway ferries arrived within minutes. All 155 people survived.

title: The girl who fell from the sky
facts: 24 December 1971, LANSA Flight 508 over the Peruvian rainforest was struck by lightning and broke apart. Juliane Koepcke, 17, fell about 3,000 m still strapped to her seat row. Injuries: broken collarbone, deep cut on her arm, eye injury, concussion. Her father was a biologist and had taught her that following water leads to people. She followed a creek to a river, and after 9 days found a lumberjack camp. 11 days alone in the jungle. She was the only survivor; up to 14 others survived the crash but died before rescue.

title: The Thai cave rescue
facts: 23 June 2018, 12 boys aged 11-16 from the Wild Boars football team and their 25-year-old assistant coach entered Tham Luang cave in Thailand; rain flooded the passages behind them. They were found alive on 2 July by British divers John Volanthen and Rick Stanton, about 2 km from the entrance on a rock shelf. Each boy was given a full-face mask, sedated, and guided out through flooded tunnels by divers, 8-10 July. Around 10,000 people helped. Former Thai Navy SEAL Saman Kunan died during the rescue; another SEAL, Beirut Pakbara, died in 2019 from an infection caught during it.

title: Shackleton's Endurance
facts: 1914-1917, Ernest Shackleton's expedition. The ship Endurance was trapped in the Weddell Sea ice in early 1915, crushed, abandoned on 27 October 1915 and sank on 21 November 1915. The men lived on the ice, then reached Elephant Island in lifeboats on 15 April 1916. Shackleton and five men sailed the small boat James Caird about 800 miles (1,300 km) to South Georgia, then Shackleton, Worsley and Crean crossed its unmapped mountains in about 36 hours, reaching Stromness on 20 May 1916. The men left on Elephant Island were rescued on 30 August 1916. All 28 men of the ship's party survived. The wreck was found on 5 March 2022.

title: Blockbuster laughed at Netflix
facts: In 2000 Netflix founders Reed Hastings and Marc Randolph offered to sell Netflix to Blockbuster for 50 million dollars; Blockbuster declined (Netflix CFO Barry McCarthy said they were laughed out of the room). Blockbuster peaked around 2004 with about 9,000 stores. It relied heavily on late fees. It filed for bankruptcy in September 2010. One privately owned Blockbuster store remains, in Bend, Oregon. Netflix became worth hundreds of billions of dollars.

title: Apollo 13
facts: April 1970. About 56 hours into the flight to the Moon, an oxygen tank in the service module exploded. Jack Swigert radioed 'Okay, Houston, we've had a problem here'; Jim Lovell repeated it. The Moon landing was cancelled. Lovell, Swigert and Fred Haise used the lunar module Aquarius as a lifeboat. Carbon dioxide rose because the command module's square filters did not fit the lunar module's round sockets; engineers on the ground designed a fix with plastic bags, cardboard and duct tape. The crew splashed down safely on 17 April 1970.

title: 33 miners underground
facts: 5 August 2010, the San Jose copper-gold mine in Chile collapsed, trapping 33 miners about 700 m underground. For 17 days nobody knew if they were alive; they rationed tiny amounts of food in a refuge. A drill finally reached them and came back with a note: 'Estamos bien en el refugio los 33' - 'We are well in the shelter, the 33'. On 13 October 2010 all 33 were pulled up one by one in a narrow capsule called Fenix 2, after 69 days underground.

title: The Dyatlov Pass incident
facts: 1-2 February 1959, nine experienced hikers led by Igor Dyatlov died on the slopes of Kholat Syakhl in the northern Urals. A tenth member, Yuri Yudin, had turned back days earlier because of illness. Their tent was cut open from the inside; they fled into temperatures of about minus 25 to minus 30 C, some in socks or barefoot. Some were found at the forest edge near the remains of a small fire. Theories ranged from the military to aliens. In 2020 Russian prosecutors named an avalanche as the official cause. In 2021 scientists Johan Gaume and Alexander Puzrin modeled a slab avalanche using snow code from Disney's Frozen. Not every question is answered.
sources: Wikipedia: Dyatlov Pass incident; Communications Earth & Environment 2021

title: Kodak invented the digital camera
facts: In 1975 Kodak engineer Steve Sasson built the first known self-contained digital camera; it was the size of a toaster, recorded 0.01 megapixel black-and-white images, and took about 23 seconds to save one image to a cassette tape. Kodak management feared it would hurt its film business. Decades later digital photography destroyed film sales, and Kodak filed for bankruptcy in January 2012.

title: 127 hours in a canyon
facts: April 2003, Aron Ralston was hiking alone in Bluejohn Canyon, Utah, and told no one where he was going. A boulder shifted and pinned his right arm against the canyon wall. He was trapped for more than five days (about 127 hours) with little water. He freed himself by amputating his forearm with a dull multi-tool, rappelled down a cliff, and hiked out until he met a family of hikers; a rescue helicopter then picked him up. His lesson: always tell someone where you are going.

title: The ghost ship Mary Celeste
facts: On 4 December 1872 the crew of the ship Dei Gratia found the Mary Celeste drifting in the Atlantic between the Azores and Portugal. Nobody was on board. Its lifeboat was missing, but the ship was seaworthy, with food and water still on board and most of its cargo of alcohol intact. Captain Benjamin Briggs, his wife, their young daughter and the crew were never found. Nobody knows for sure why they left.
